title: Fast rhythm with a pulse
note: Fictional patient. Doses and energies are quoted from the 2025 AHA guidelines (and the ERC where named) for recognition; your unit protocol, crash-cart stock and the attending nephrologist come first. Simulation success is an educational result, not a prediction of patient survival.
intro: Mr. Felix Domingo, 52, dialyzes through a tunneled catheter. Halfway through his session he reports palpitations. He is alert, talking, pressure 118/72. You are the physician-on-duty.

n1.prompt: Is he stable, and what first?

choices.text: Stable: 12-lead ECG, stop fluid removal per protocol, vagal maneuver, then adenosine per protocol if it persists.
choices.feedback: Stable regular narrow tachycardia: vagal maneuvers, then adenosine (COR 1).
No signs of compromise; cardioversion is for instability.
choices.then: You pause and treat him as stable.

n2.scene: Vagal maneuvers fail. He has only the dialysis catheter for access.

choices.text: Aspirate the catheter lock, flush; give the dose the physician decides for a central line (the guideline notes 1 mg may be adequate), as a rapid push with a flush; warn him about a brief pause.
choices.feedback: A dialysis catheter is a central line: lock first, and the dose decision changes.

choices.text: Push 12 mg straight into the catheter limb with the lock still in it.
choices.feedback: This pushes heparin or citrate lock into him and gives a large central dose.
choices.then: The circuit nurse stops you, aspirates the lock, and you choose a central-line dose.

n3.scene: After adenosine, the rhythm briefly slows, then returns at 180. Now his pressure is 76/40 and he is confused.

choices.text: Unstable: synchronized cardioversion per protocol (sedate if feasible), sync markers confirmed on each R wave, everyone clear.
choices.feedback: Persistent tachyarrhythmia with hypotension and confusion needs synchronized cardioversion.
He is now unstable; drugs must not delay cardioversion.
An unsynchronized shock can land on the T wave and cause VF; use sync for a tachycardia with a pulse.
choices.then: You switch the device to sync before the shock.

n4.scene: He is in sinus rhythm, alert, pressure 112/70.

choices.text: Keep him monitored; the physician-on-duty and attending decide whether to resume, return the blood or end; check potassium, magnesium, and the catheter tip position if suspected.
choices.feedback: Rhythm changes around dialysis need a cause review before restarting.

choices.text: Restart fluid removal at the original rate.
choices.feedback: Restarting without review may trigger it again; the attending decides.
choices.then: The attending lowers the fluid goal and asks for electrolytes.

end.title: 12:30 p.m.
end.text: Mr. Domingo finishes a shortened session with a reduced fluid goal and is referred for cardiology review.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Stable or unstable decides the path.
  • Adenosine through a dialysis catheter: aspirate the lock; central-line dose decided by the physician.
  • Synchronized for tachycardia with a pulse; unsynchronized only for pulseless or polymorphic VT.
